pattern.note: The official CLAT PG paper has 120 MCQs/120 marks/120 minutes, built on passage-based questions. This mock is extended to 150 questions as requested; scale to 120 by dropping any 5 passages if you want exact parity.

instructions: Each question carries 1 mark; 0.25 marks deducted for each wrong answer.
Answer from the passage and the legal principles stated or implied; read every option.
Current-affairs passages summarise developments up to the date of preparation; verify case details before citing in exam answers.

passages.title: Hart's Concept of Law: Rules, Recognition and Obligation
passages.passage: H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law (1961) begins by rejecting John Austin's account of law as the commands of a determinate sovereign, backed by threats and habitually obeyed. Hart argued that this model cannot explain power-conferring rules, such as those governing the making of wills or contracts, which command nothing yet are plainly law; nor can it explain the continuity of law when one sovereign is succeeded by another. In its place Hart offers the union of primary and secondary rules. Primary rules impose duties. Secondary rules are rules about rules: the rule of recognition identifies which rules count as law; rules of change allow rules to be made, altered or repealed; and rules of adjudication empower particular persons to determine authoritatively whether a rule has been broken. The rule of recognition is ultimate in the sense that its validity cannot be derived from any higher rule; its existence is a question of fact, namely whether officials in practice use it as the common standard for identifying law. Hart distinguishes the external from the internal point of view. An observer who merely records that people usually behave in a certain way takes the external view; a participant who treats the rule as a reason for her own conduct and a standard for criticising others takes the internal view. Officials must take the internal view towards the rule of recognition, while ordinary citizens may merely obey. Hart also separates 'being obliged' from 'having an obligation': a person who hands over money to a gunman is obliged to do so, but does not thereby have an obligation. In the Postscript, Hart accepted that a rule of recognition may incorporate moral criteria of validity ('inclusive' or 'soft' positivism), whereas Joseph Raz and other 'exclusive' positivists insist that the existence and content of law can always be identified without recourse to moral argument.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT identified by Hart as a deficiency in Austin's model?

options.A: It fails to appreciate that the validity of law depends upon its moral content
options.B: It reduces all law to commands backed by threats
options.C: It cannot explain the continuity of law after a change of sovereign
options.D: It cannot account for rules that confer powers on private persons

questions.explanation: Hart criticised Austin on power-conferring rules, continuity and the command-threat model. Austin was himself a positivist; Hart did not fault him for ignoring a moral test of validity.

questions.question: The rule of recognition is described as 'ultimate' because

options.A: it is the most morally defensible rule in the system
options.B: it is enforced by the strongest sanction
options.C: it can be changed only by a rule of adjudication
options.D: its validity is not derived from a higher rule and its existence rests on the practice of officials

questions.explanation: The passage states that the rule's validity cannot be derived from any higher rule and that its existence is a question of fact, namely official practice.

questions.question: In State X, judges in different provinces apply different personal tests to decide which enactments are law, and each treats his test as a matter of private preference. Citizens, however, obey most enactments. On Hart's theory, which conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: A legal system exists because citizens generally obey
options.B: A legal system exists because primary rules are in force
options.C: A legal system is doubtful because officials do not share a common standard of recognition
options.D: A legal system exists only if the rules are morally just

questions.explanation: Citizen obedience alone is insufficient. Officials must collectively accept a common rule of recognition as a public standard; its absence defeats the existence of a legal system.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best illustration of the 'internal point of view'?

options.A: A foreign lawyer who predicts what a court will do
options.B: A citizen who pays tax only because he fears prosecution
options.C: A judge who treats a statute as a reason for her decision and criticises a colleague who departs from it
options.D: A sociologist who counts how many motorists stop at red lights

questions.explanation: The internal view involves treating the rule as a reason for action and a standard of criticism. The other options reflect the external view or mere obedience.

questions.question: Country Z's constitution declares that any statute violating equal human dignity is invalid. Which statement best captures the positivist debate on this provision?

options.A: Both inclusive and exclusive positivists must deny that this is law
options.B: Inclusive positivists may accept that the rule of recognition itself incorporates a moral criterion of validity, while exclusive positivists deny that a moral test can be a condition of legal validity
options.C: Exclusive positivists accept the provision as a criterion of validity but inclusive positivists reject it
options.D: Neither school can recognise a written constitution

questions.explanation: Per the passage, soft positivism allows moral criteria to be part of the rule of recognition; Raz's exclusive positivism requires law's existence and content to be identifiable without moral argument.

questions.question: A shopkeeper pays 'protection money' to a local gang solely out of fear of violence. Applying the distinction drawn in the passage, he is

options.A: neither obliged nor under an obligation
options.B: obliged to pay, but does not thereby have an obligation
options.C: both obliged and under an obligation
options.D: under a legal obligation to pay

questions.explanation: The gunman example shows that coercion creates being obliged; having an obligation involves acceptance of a rule as a standard.

passages.title: Governors, Bills and the Limits of Judicial Timelines
passages.passage: Article 200 of the Constitution provides that when a Bill passed by a State Legislature is presented to the Governor, the Governor may assent to it, withhold assent, or reserve it for the consideration of the President. The first proviso adds that, except for a Money Bill, the Governor may return the Bill as soon as possible with a message requesting reconsideration; if the House passes it again, with or without amendments, the Governor shall not withhold assent. The Article prescribes no time-limit, which led to prolonged inaction by Governors in several States. In April 2025, in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, a two-judge bench held that the Governor's refusal to act on re-passed Bills was illegal, read timelines into the Article (generally one to three months, depending on the course adopted) and, invoking Article 142, declared ten Bills to have been 'deemed' assented to. The President then made a reference under Article 143, asking whether courts can impose timelines or deem assent. In November 2025, a Constitution Bench of five judges delivered its advisory opinion. It held that the Governor has three constitutionally available courses: grant assent, reserve the Bill for the President, or withhold assent and return a non-money Bill with a message; the Governor cannot simply sit on a Bill indefinitely, because that would reduce the elected legislature to a supplicant and permit an informal 'pocket veto'. At the same time, the Bench held that courts cannot prescribe rigid timelines where the Constitution has chosen to prescribe none, nor deem a Bill to be assented to, since doing so would substitute the judiciary for a constitutional functionary. Article 142, it said, cannot be used to supplant the Constitution's allocation of powers. It nevertheless accepted that where inaction is prolonged, unexplained and indefinite, a court may issue a limited direction that the Governor decide within a reasonable time, without commenting on the merits of the decision.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a course open to the Governor under Article 200, as explained in the passage?

options.A: Withholding assent to a non-money Bill and returning it with a message
options.B: Reserving the Bill for the consideration of the President
options.C: Granting assent to the Bill
options.D: Withholding assent and retaining the Bill indefinitely without any communication

questions.explanation: The Bench held that indefinite retention amounts to an impermissible pocket veto; only the three courses listed are available.

questions.question: According to the November 2025 opinion, the concept of 'deemed assent' is

options.A: permissible if the delay exceeds three months
options.B: valid only for Money Bills
options.C: valid, since Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice
options.D: impermissible, because it substitutes the judiciary for a constitutional functionary

questions.explanation: The Bench held courts cannot deem assent, and Article 142 cannot supplant the constitutional allocation of powers.

questions.question: Why, according to the passage, did the Constitution Bench decline to fix rigid timelines?

options.A: Because Governors enjoy absolute immunity under Article 361
options.B: Because timelines apply only to the President
options.C: Because the Constitution deliberately prescribes no time-limit and fixing one would amount to rewriting the text
options.D: Because the State Legislature can always re-pass a Bill

questions.explanation: The Bench reasoned that courts cannot impose rigid timelines where the Constitution has chosen to prescribe none.

questions.question: A Governor has taken no decision on a non-money Bill for more than two years and offers no reason. Consistent with the opinion, the appropriate judicial response is

options.A: to direct the Governor to decide within a reasonable time without examining the merits of the decision
options.B: to declare that the Bill has become law
options.C: to assent to the Bill on the Governor's behalf
options.D: to dismiss any petition as non-justiciable in all circumstances

questions.explanation: Prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction permits a limited direction to decide within a reasonable time; merits remain outside review.

questions.question: In the passage, the expression 'pocket veto' refers to

options.A: the legislature's power to re-pass a Bill
options.B: the President's power to return a Bill for reconsideration
options.C: the Governor's power to reserve a Bill for the President
options.D: the effective defeat of a Bill by keeping it pending indefinitely without a decision

questions.explanation: The Bench used the phrase for informal defeat of a Bill through unlimited inaction.

questions.question: Which statement about the Article 143 reference is most accurate on the basis of the passage and the Constitution?

options.A: The reference can be used to reverse an earlier judgment between the same parties
options.B: The Court is bound to answer every question and its opinion operates as a judgment inter partes
options.C: The reference seeks the Court's advisory opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance, and is not a decision in a dispute between parties
options.D: The reference can be made only by a Governor

questions.explanation: Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction; the Court gives an opinion on a question referred by the President and does not adjudicate a lis between parties.

passages.title: The New Criminal Codes: BNS, BNSS and BSA
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Evidence Act respectively. The BNS does not retain the offence of sedition; instead Section 152 penalises acts which endanger the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, a formulation critics argue is as broad as the old provision. It introduces organised crime (Section 111) and terrorist acts (Section 113) as offences in the general penal code, recognises community service as a punishment for certain petty offences, and criminalises sexual intercourse obtained by deceitful means, including a false promise of marriage (Section 69). Murder committed by a group of five or more persons acting in concert on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief attracts death or imprisonment for life (Section 103(2)). The BNSS permits 'Zero FIR', allowing information about a cognisable offence to be registered at any police station irrespective of territorial jurisdiction and then transferred. It also provides for electronic filing of information, which must be signed by the informant within three days. Where an investigation cannot be completed in the usual period, detention before the charge-sheet is limited to sixty days, or ninety days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more; police custody of up to fifteen days may be authorised in whole or in part during the first forty or sixty days of that period, respectively. The BNSS also allows trial of a proclaimed offender in absentia, after charges are framed and a waiting period of ninety days has elapsed. Under the BSA, electronic records are treated as documents and may be admitted as primary evidence, but a certificate in the prescribed form, signed by the person in charge of the device and an expert, is required.

questions.question: Which of the following is correctly stated on the basis of the passage?

options.A: Community service is a punishment for all offences under the BNS
options.B: Section 152 of the BNS penalises acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
options.C: Sedition has been retained in the BNS in an unchanged form
options.D: Organised crime continues to be dealt with only under special statutes

questions.explanation: The passage states that Section 152 replaces sedition with an offence based on endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity; the other options are contrary to the text.

questions.question: An accused is arrested for an offence punishable with imprisonment for life. Police custody may be authorised

options.A: for up to fifteen days, in whole or in part, during the first sixty days of detention
options.B: only after the charge-sheet is filed
options.C: for up to fifteen days, only in the first forty days of detention
options.D: for an unlimited period if the Magistrate is satisfied

questions.explanation: For offences punishable with death, life or ten years or more, the period is ninety days and police custody may be authorised in the first sixty days.

questions.question: Which of the following is a condition for trial in absentia under the BNSS, as described in the passage?

options.A: The informant must have consented in writing
options.B: The trial may begin before charges are framed
options.C: The accused must have been convicted earlier
options.D: The accused must be a proclaimed offender and the trial may proceed after charges are framed and ninety days have elapsed

questions.explanation: Trial in absentia is available against a proclaimed offender after charges are framed and a waiting period of ninety days.

questions.question: A resident of Delhi is robbed in Jaipur and reports the matter at a Delhi police station. Under the 'Zero FIR' mechanism

options.A: the Delhi police must investigate and cannot transfer the case
options.B: the information may be registered only if the Magistrate permits
options.C: the information may be registered at the Delhi station and then transferred to the station having jurisdiction
options.D: the police must refuse as Delhi has no territorial jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Zero FIR permits registration irrespective of territorial jurisdiction, followed by transfer.

questions.question: A prosecutor wishes to rely on a copy of CCTV footage stored on a hard drive. On the basis of the passage, which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The footage is inadmissible because it is not paper
options.B: The footage is admissible only as secondary evidence of no value
options.C: The footage may be admitted as primary evidence, but a certificate in the prescribed form signed by the person in charge of the device and an expert is required
options.D: No certificate is needed if a police officer testifies

questions.explanation: The BSA treats electronic records as documents but requires the prescribed certificate by the person in charge and an expert.

questions.question: Three persons beat a man to death solely because of his caste. Which provision is most appropriately attracted on the facts?

options.A: Section 103(2), because the killing was caste-based
options.B: Section 103(1), the general offence of murder, because Section 103(2) requires a group of five or more
options.C: Section 111, organised crime, because more than one person is involved
options.D: Section 113, because it is a terrorist act

questions.explanation: The caste-based group-murder provision requires five or more persons acting in concert. With three, liability falls under the general murder provision.

passages.title: Data Protection and the Right to Privacy
passages.passage: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Bench held that privacy is a fundamental right under Articles 14, 19 and 21. A restriction on privacy must satisfy a test of proportionality: it must be backed by law, pursue a legitimate State aim, bear a rational connection to that aim and be necessary in the sense that no less intrusive alternative exists, and be accompanied by procedural safeguards against abuse. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is India's first horizontal data protection statute. It speaks of the Data Principal, the individual to whom the data relates, and the Data Fiduciary, which determines the purpose and means of processing. Processing is lawful principally on the basis of consent, which must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, though the Act also lists 'legitimate uses' such as compliance with law and medical emergencies where consent is not required. For a child, defined as a person below eighteen years, verifiable parental consent is required, and the Act bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. The Data Protection Board of India adjudicates breaches, and penalties may extend to Rs 250 crore for failure to take reasonable security safeguards. Critics point to Section 17, under which the Central Government may exempt State instrumentalities from the Act by notification in the interests of matters such as sovereignty, security and public order, and to Section 44(3), which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 so that personal information may be refused without the earlier balancing of the public interest. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 and are being brought into force in phases: the provisions relating to the Board take effect at once, those on Consent Managers after twelve months and the core obligations of Data Fiduciaries after eighteen months.

questions.question: An online pharmacy decides what patient data to collect and for what purpose. In the vocabulary of the Act, the pharmacy and the patient are respectively

options.A: Data Fiduciary and Data Principal
options.B: Data Fiduciary and Consent Manager
options.C: Consent Manager and Data Principal
options.D: Data Principal and Data Fiduciary

questions.explanation: The entity determining purpose and means is the Data Fiduciary; the individual to whom data relates is the Data Principal.

questions.question: A gaming app uses a fifteen-year-old's browsing history, with her parent's consent, to show her targeted advertisements. Under the Act as described, this is

options.A: permissible only if the Board is informed
options.B: impermissible, because targeted advertising directed at children is barred
options.C: lawful, because parental consent was obtained
options.D: lawful, because she is above thirteen

questions.explanation: The Act bars targeted advertising and behavioural monitoring directed at persons below eighteen; parental consent does not cure the bar.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of the proportionality test as stated in the passage?

options.A: Necessity, with no less intrusive alternative
options.B: Existence of a law
options.C: A legitimate State aim
options.D: Prior approval of Parliament for every individual restriction

questions.explanation: The passage lists legality, legitimate aim, rational connection and necessity, and procedural safeguards; individual parliamentary approval is not required.

questions.question: The criticism directed at Section 44(3) of the Act is that it

options.A: removes the balancing of public interest when refusing disclosure of personal information
options.B: repeals Section 8 of the RTI Act altogether
options.C: extends the Right to Information Act to private companies
options.D: makes all personal information public

questions.explanation: The amendment to Section 8(1)(j) allows refusal of personal information without the earlier public-interest balancing.

questions.question: A Data Fiduciary fails to adopt reasonable security safeguards and a breach occurs. The maximum penalty indicated in the passage is

options.A: Rs 50 crore
options.B: Rs 100 crore
options.C: Rs 250 crore
options.D: Rs 500 crore

questions.explanation: The passage states penalties may extend to Rs 250 crore for this failure.

questions.question: Fourteen months after notification of the Rules, which of the following has most likely taken effect?

options.A: Only the provisions relating to the Board
options.B: The provisions relating to the Board and to Consent Managers, but not yet the core obligations of Data Fiduciaries
options.C: None, as the Rules are yet to commence
options.D: All provisions, including core obligations

questions.explanation: Board provisions were immediate and Consent Manager provisions apply after twelve months; core obligations follow after eighteen months.

passages.title: Dworkin's Principles and Fuller's Inner Morality of Law
passages.passage: Ronald Dworkin attacked Hart's positivism on the ground that law consists not only of rules but also of principles, standards that judges are obliged to consider because they express a requirement of justice, fairness or morality. In Riggs v. Palmer, a New York court refused to let an heir who had murdered his grandfather take under the will, invoking the principle that no one should profit from his own wrong, though the statute of wills contained no such exception. Dworkin argued that rules apply in an all-or-nothing fashion, whereas principles have a dimension of weight and may be outweighed by other principles without ceasing to be valid. Because principles are not validated by their pedigree, that is, by enactment in accordance with a rule of recognition, Dworkin claimed that positivism cannot explain how judges decide hard cases. He proposed that law is a matter of integrity: judges should decide hard cases by constructing the interpretation that best fits and justifies the existing legal materials, an ideal embodied in his imagined judge Hercules, and he defended the 'right answer thesis'. Lon Fuller, by contrast, approached law through its 'inner morality', eight desiderata without which the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to rules fails: generality; promulgation; prospectivity; clarity; consistency; possibility of compliance; constancy through time; and congruence between declared rules and official action. Fuller argued that a total failure in any of these does not produce a bad legal system but no legal system at all. In the celebrated debate arising from the post-war 'grudge informer' case, Hart maintained that a wicked enactment may nonetheless be valid law, though it may be morally right to disobey it, whereas Fuller contended that fidelity to law could not be separated from the moral qualities of legality.

questions.question: According to Dworkin, the essential difference between rules and principles is that

options.A: rules are moral while principles are legal
options.B: rules apply in an all-or-nothing way while principles have weight and may be outweighed
options.C: rules are applied only by Parliament while principles are applied by judges
options.D: principles are enacted while rules are customary

questions.explanation: The passage states that rules apply all-or-nothing whereas principles have a dimension of weight.

questions.question: Riggs v. Palmer is used by Dworkin to show that

options.A: a will can never be revoked
options.B: judges may disregard statutes at will
options.C: legal systems contain principles that influence decisions even though no rule of recognition validated them by pedigree
options.D: courts must follow the literal text of statutes

questions.explanation: The court invoked a principle not found in the statute, illustrating Dworkin's point about principles beyond pedigree.

questions.question: A Government publishes an order only in a sealed file known to officials and punishes citizens for breach of its terms. Which of Fuller's desiderata is most directly violated?

options.A: Constancy through time
options.B: Prospectivity
options.C: Promulgation
options.D: Possibility of compliance

questions.explanation: Secret rules which citizens cannot know offend the requirement of promulgation.

questions.question: A statute requires every taxpayer to file returns within 24 hours of the close of the financial year, a task that is physically impossible for most. Which desideratum is chiefly offended?

options.A: Possibility of compliance
options.B: Clarity
options.C: Congruence
options.D: Generality

questions.explanation: Rules requiring the impossible violate the requirement that compliance be possible.

questions.question: Which statement best represents the difference between Hart and Fuller in the 'grudge informer' debate?

options.A: Hart denied that the enactment was a statute; Fuller accepted it as law
options.B: Hart held that a wicked enactment may be valid law but disobeyed; Fuller held that legality has inherent moral qualities
options.C: Both held that the enactment was not law
options.D: Both held that the enactment was binding on judges without exception

questions.explanation: Hart separated validity from morality; Fuller insisted that legality carries an inner morality.

questions.question: Which of the following would Dworkin most likely accept?

options.A: In hard cases, judges should seek the interpretation that best fits and morally justifies the existing legal materials
options.B: Judges in hard cases exercise unfettered discretion, in which they legislate
options.C: The identification of law depends solely on social facts of pedigree
options.D: Judges should be bound by a rigid mechanical application of precedents

questions.explanation: This is law as integrity, in contrast to the positivist discretion thesis.

passages.title: Sub-classification of Scheduled Castes and the Creamy Layer
passages.passage: Article 341 empowers the President to specify the castes to be deemed Scheduled Castes in each State, and Articles 15(4) and 16(4) enable the State to make special provisions and reservations for backward classes inadequately represented in services. In E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2004), a five-judge Bench held that Scheduled Castes form a homogeneous group and that sub-classifying them for reservation would amount to tampering with the Presidential List. In State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024), a seven-judge Bench, by a majority of six to one, overruled Chinnaiah. The majority reasoned that Article 341 merely identifies castes for the purpose of deeming them Scheduled Castes and does not prevent the State from differentiating among them for the purposes of reservation, and that historical and empirical evidence shows that some Scheduled Castes are more disadvantaged than others. The Court held, however, that sub-classification must not be arbitrary. The State must justify it by 'quantifiable and demonstrable data' showing the inadequate representation of the sub-class in services, rather than by political expediency or mere assumption; the State cannot reserve the entire quota for a single sub-class, and its decisions remain open to judicial review. In separate opinions, some judges, including Justice B.R. Gavai, suggested that the 'creamy layer' principle, which in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) was applied to Other Backward Classes, should also be applied to identify and exclude the advanced among Scheduled Castes and Tribes; this suggestion was not part of the operative holding of the Bench. The dissenting judge held that the Presidential List is a closed one, and that any alteration of it lies exclusively within the power of Parliament under Article 341(2).

questions.question: The decision in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh overruled which earlier decision?

options.A: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
options.B: E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
options.C: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
options.D: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

questions.explanation: The passage records that the seven-judge Bench overruled Chinnaiah (2004).

questions.question: According to the majority, a State seeking to sub-classify Scheduled Castes must

options.A: obtain the prior consent of Parliament
options.B: rely on quantifiable and demonstrable data showing inadequate representation of the sub-class
options.C: reserve the entire quota for the most backward sub-class
options.D: apply the creamy-layer test in all cases

questions.explanation: The majority insisted on empirical justification and rejected political expediency.

questions.question: A State reserves the whole Scheduled Caste quota in a recruitment for one sub-caste, without data. On the passage, this action is

options.A: valid if the sub-caste is the most numerous
options.B: valid as sub-classification is now allowed
options.C: open to invalidation, as the State cannot reserve the entire quota for one sub-class and must rely on data
options.D: invalid only if Parliament amends Article 341

questions.explanation: Both limits stated in the passage are violated: no data and exclusive reservation.

questions.question: The majority's reasoning on Article 341 is that the Article

options.A: freezes the Presidential List and precludes any State action
options.B: gives States power to modify the list
options.C: merely identifies castes to be deemed Scheduled Castes and does not prohibit differentiated treatment for reservation
options.D: applies only to Scheduled Tribes

questions.explanation: The passage records this reasoning in explaining why Chinnaiah was overruled.

questions.question: The status of the creamy-layer suggestion for Scheduled Castes in the judgment is best described as

options.A: an overruling of Indra Sawhney
options.B: the unanimous view of all seven judges
options.C: an observation in separate opinions, not part of the operative holding
options.D: a binding ratio of the seven-judge Bench

questions.explanation: The passage states that the suggestion was not part of the operative holding.

questions.question: Which of the following would the dissenting judge most likely agree with?

options.A: The creamy layer must be applied to every reserved category
options.B: States may freely sub-classify without data
options.C: Only Parliament can alter the Presidential List under Article 341(2), and sub-classification by States amounts to such an alteration
options.D: Chinnaiah was wrongly decided

questions.explanation: The dissent held the list to be closed and alterable only by Parliament.

passages.title: The Tenth Schedule and the Speaker's Delay
passages.passage: The Tenth Schedule, inserted in 1985, provides for the disqualification of a member of Parliament or a State Legislature who voluntarily gives up the membership of his party or defies its whip on a vote. The Schedule recognises a merger only where not less than two-thirds of the legislature party agree to it. Under paragraph 6, the question of disqualification is to be decided by the Speaker or Chairman of the House. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), a Constitution Bench upheld the Schedule but struck down paragraph 7, which barred the jurisdiction of courts, and held that the Speaker, in exercising this power, acts as a tribunal whose decisions are subject to limited judicial review, for example for mala fides, perversity or violation of constitutional mandates. Experience has shown that Speakers, belonging to the ruling party in most cases, have sometimes sat on disqualification petitions until the term of the House expires, rendering them infructuous. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Hon'ble Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020), the Supreme Court held that Speakers should ordinarily decide such petitions within three months and urged Parliament to consider vesting the power in an independent tribunal. In July 2025, hearing petitions concerning legislators in Telangana who had defected after being elected on the ticket of one party, the Court directed the Speaker to decide the petitions within three months, observing that the Speaker is not immune from judicial scrutiny and that allowing petitions to be delayed until the term of the Assembly lapses would defeat the constitutional policy against defection. The Court added that Parliament should reconsider whether the Speaker, who remains a member of a political party, is the appropriate authority for adjudicating such disputes.

questions.question: The ground on which paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was struck down in Kihoto Hollohan was that it

options.A: made the Speaker's decision appealable to the President
options.B: excluded the jurisdiction of courts
options.C: permitted mergers without a two-thirds majority
options.D: provided for disqualification without a hearing

questions.explanation: The passage states that paragraph 7 barred judicial jurisdiction and was struck down.

questions.question: In the passage, the Speaker deciding a disqualification petition is described as

options.A: an appellate authority over the High Court
options.B: a purely legislative authority immune from review
options.C: a tribunal whose decision is subject to limited judicial review
options.D: an executive officer of the Government

questions.explanation: Kihoto Hollohan held that the Speaker acts as a tribunal whose decisions can be reviewed on limited grounds.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a delay by the Speaker is considered constitutionally problematic?

options.A: It increases the number of petitions
options.B: It transfers jurisdiction to the High Court
options.C: It permits mergers with less than two-thirds support
options.D: It may render the petition infructuous when the House's term expires, thereby defeating the anti-defection policy

questions.explanation: The passage identifies infructuousness through delay as defeating the constitutional policy.

questions.question: A group of 40% of a legislature party joins another party and claims that it constitutes a 'merger'. On the passage, the claim is

options.A: valid if the Speaker approves
options.B: valid, since a merger requires a simple majority
options.C: invalid only if the whip is defied
options.D: invalid, since a merger requires the agreement of at least two-thirds of the legislature party

questions.explanation: The Schedule recognises a merger only with at least two-thirds of the legislature party.

questions.question: What was the direction of the Supreme Court in the July 2025 Telangana matter?

options.A: The petitions were transferred to the Election Commission
options.B: The Speaker was directed to decide the petitions within three months
options.C: The matter was referred to a tribunal created by the Court
options.D: The Speaker was directed to disqualify the legislators

questions.explanation: The Court directed a decision within three months and observed that the Speaker is not immune from scrutiny.

questions.question: Which proposition is the most consistent with the passage?

options.A: Courts may fix a reasonable time for the Speaker to decide, although the Schedule itself prescribes none, because inaction can defeat constitutional policy
options.B: Parliament is bound to constitute an independent tribunal
options.C: The Speaker's decision on disqualification is final under paragraph 7
options.D: Judicial review of a Speaker's decision is barred in all cases

questions.explanation: The Court, while leaving the Speaker to decide, laid down a time frame by reason of the risk of defeat of the anti-defection policy; the Court only urged Parliament to reconsider the authority.

passages.title: Mineral Rights, Royalty and Fiscal Federalism
passages.passage: Entry 54 of the Union List permits Parliament to regulate mines and mineral development to the extent that Parliament declares it expedient in the public interest, while Entry 50 of the State List empowers the States to tax mineral rights 'subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development'. Entry 49 permits States to tax lands and buildings. In India Cement Ltd v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990), a seven-judge Bench held that royalty on minerals is a tax, and that a State cess on royalty was therefore beyond the competence of the State because it amounted to a tax on a tax which the State could not impose. A clerical error later suggested that royalty was not a tax, and the controversy was referred to a nine-judge Bench. In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (July 2024), the Bench by a majority of eight to one held that royalty is a contractual payment made to the lessor for the right to extract minerals and not a tax. It further held that Parliament's power under Entry 54 does not include the power to tax mineral rights, which falls to the States under Entry 50, though Parliament may impose limitations by legislation on mineral development, and that the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 does not by itself limit that power. The dissenting judge would have held that allowing States to tax minerals would disturb the national mineral policy. In August 2024, the Court allowed States to recover the past dues from 1 April 2005, to be paid in instalments over twelve years, without interest or penalty. Separately, in Mohit Minerals v. Union of India (2022), the Court held that recommendations of the GST Council are not binding on the Union and States, being only persuasive, since Article 246A confers concurrent power on both to legislate on GST, and cooperative federalism requires dialogue and not dominance.

questions.question: According to the passage, in the 2024 decision, royalty on minerals was held to be

options.A: an exempt category of income
options.B: a cess imposed by Parliament
options.C: a tax within the meaning of Entry 50
options.D: a contractual payment made to the lessor and not a tax

questions.explanation: The majority held royalty to be a contractual payment for the right to extract minerals.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the effect of the 2024 decision on the power of the States?

options.A: States may tax mineral rights under Entry 50, subject to limitations Parliament may impose by law relating to mineral development
options.B: States may not levy any tax on minerals
options.C: States may tax minerals only after Presidential consent
options.D: Only Parliament may tax mineral rights under Entry 54

questions.explanation: The Court held that Entry 50 is the source of the States' power, which is subject to Parliament's limits.

questions.question: Which of the following decisions is overruled by the 2024 judgment on the point of royalty being a tax?

options.A: Mohit Minerals v. Union of India
options.B: India Cement Ltd v. State of Tamil Nadu
options.C: Steel Authority of India v. State
options.D: None of these

questions.explanation: India Cement had held royalty to be a tax; the nine-judge Bench held otherwise.

questions.question: The arrangement allowed by the Court for the recovery of past dues from the States' tax was

options.A: Recovery only for the future
options.B: No recovery at all
options.C: Immediate full payment with interest
options.D: Recovery from 1 April 2005 in instalments over twelve years without interest or penalty

questions.explanation: This is as described in the passage.

questions.question: The Court in Mohit Minerals held that GST Council recommendations are

options.A: persuasive only, in view of Article 246A and cooperative federalism
options.B: binding on both the Union and the States
options.C: binding only on the Union
options.D: binding only on the States

questions.explanation: The passage states they are not binding but persuasive.

questions.question: The dissenting judge's concern, as reflected in the passage, was that

options.A: the case should have been decided by a smaller Bench
options.B: royalty should be treated as a tax
options.C: India Cement was rightly overruled
options.D: allowing States to tax minerals would undermine national mineral policy

questions.explanation: The passage records the concern about disturbance of national mineral policy.

passages.title: 'Bulldozer Justice' and Due Process
passages.passage: In recent years, several State authorities have demolished the homes and properties of persons accused of crimes, often without prior notice and on the allegation that the structures were unauthorised. In In Re: Directions in the matter of demolition of structures (November 2024), the Supreme Court condemned the practice. It held that the executive cannot act as a judge and determine the guilt of an accused, and then punish him by demolishing his home; such action violates the separation of powers and the right to shelter, which is part of the right to life under Article 21. Reiterating that punishing the family of the accused for the alleged acts of one member is unconstitutional, the Court laid down binding, pan-India directions under Article 142. No demolition may proceed without a show-cause notice served by registered post and affixed on the structure, giving at least fifteen days' time or the time required by the local municipal law, whichever is longer. The notice must specify the nature of the unauthorised construction, the particular violation and the grounds for demolition, and must provide an opportunity of a personal hearing. The final order must be reasoned and communicated, and the owner must be given fifteen days to challenge it or remove the structure voluntarily before any demolition. The process must be videographed and notified on a digital portal. Officials who violate the directions are liable for contempt and may be personally required to restore the property at their own cost and pay compensation. The Court clarified that the directions do not apply to unauthorised structures in public places such as roads, streets, footpaths, railway lines or water bodies, or to cases where a court has itself ordered demolition.

questions.question: The principal constitutional objection of the Court to demolition as punishment was that it

options.A: is permitted if the accused is convicted
options.B: violates the separation of powers and the right to shelter under Article 21
options.C: violates Article 19(1)(g) alone
options.D: violates only municipal law

questions.explanation: The passage records both separation of powers and Article 21 as the basis.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the procedural safeguards mentioned in the passage?

options.A: Prior sanction of the High Court for each demolition
options.B: A reasoned final order with fifteen days to challenge or remove the structure
options.C: A show-cause notice by registered post and affixed on the structure
options.D: A personal hearing

questions.explanation: The High Court's prior sanction is not required; the other three safeguards are listed.

questions.question: A municipality wishes to remove a hut built on a railway track. According to the passage, the directions

options.A: apply only if the occupant has a criminal record
options.B: apply fully and the municipality must follow every step
options.C: do not apply to unauthorised structures on railway lines
options.D: apply only if the hut is more than ten years old

questions.explanation: Public places such as railway lines are specifically carved out.

questions.question: The Court's reference to the family of an accused being punished suggests that

options.A: the family's liability depends on whether it owns the house
options.B: collective punishment is acceptable in grave cases
options.C: the Court has no view on the matter
options.D: punishing relatives for the acts of an accused is unconstitutional

questions.explanation: The passage records that such punishment of the family is unconstitutional.

questions.question: An officer demolishes a house without notice, in breach of the directions. Which consequence is indicated in the passage?

options.A: Only the State Government can be held liable
options.B: The owner may only seek a fresh notice
options.C: The officer may be liable for contempt and be required to restore the property at personal cost and pay compensation
options.D: The officer has immunity as he acted in good faith

questions.explanation: Personal liability, contempt and restoration at the officer's cost are specified.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the constitutional principle on which the decision rests?

options.A: Article 142 allows the Court to abolish municipal law
options.B: Demolition is a civil remedy and needs no safeguards
options.C: Adjudication of guilt and imposition of punishment belong to the judiciary, and State action affecting shelter must follow fair, reasoned procedure
options.D: Administrative expediency prevails over procedure in cases of crime

questions.explanation: The decision is rooted in separation of powers and due process under Article 21.

passages.title: Grounds of Arrest, Bail and Special Statutes
passages.passage: Article 22(1) of the Constitution provides that no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest, nor be denied the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice. In Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India (2023), the Supreme Court held that the Enforcement Directorate must furnish the written grounds of arrest to the arrested person under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), and that merely reading them out is insufficient. In Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024), the same requirement was applied to arrests under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. In Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra (2025), the Court held that the requirement applies to arrests under all penal statutes, that the grounds must be communicated in writing in a language the arrestee understands, and that non-compliance renders the arrest illegal and vitiates the subsequent remand. Section 45 of the PMLA imposes 'twin conditions' for bail: the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. In Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb (2021) and in Manish Sisodia v. Directorate of Enforcement (2024), the Court has held that prolonged incarceration without trial offends Article 21, and that the principle 'bail is the rule and jail the exception' applies even to special statutes with stringent conditions. Constitutional courts may therefore grant bail notwithstanding statutory restrictions where the trial is delayed and the accused has suffered long incarceration.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with the Supreme Court's decision in Pankaj Bansal?

options.A: The requirement applies only to arrests by the police
options.B: The Enforcement Directorate must give the written grounds of arrest to the arrested person
options.C: The grounds need be given only to the arrestee's relatives
options.D: Oral communication of the grounds of arrest is always sufficient

questions.explanation: The Court held that written grounds must be furnished and mere reading out is insufficient.

questions.question: In Mihir Rajesh Shah, the Court held that failure to supply the grounds of arrest in writing

options.A: is a mere irregularity
options.B: renders the arrest illegal and vitiates the remand
options.C: has no bearing on the remand order
options.D: entitles the accused to compensation only

questions.explanation: The passage states that non-compliance renders the arrest illegal and vitiates the remand.

questions.question: A person arrested for an ordinary offence under the BNS is told the grounds orally and is not given any written grounds. According to the passage, the arrest is

options.A: open to challenge as illegal, since the written grounds requirement applies to all penal statutes
options.B: valid because the requirement applies only to PMLA arrests
options.C: valid because the requirement applies only to UAPA arrests
options.D: valid if the arrestee is represented by a lawyer

questions.explanation: Mihir Rajesh Shah extended the requirement to all penal statutes.

questions.question: The 'twin conditions' under Section 45 of the PMLA require the court to be satisfied that

options.A: the accused has been in custody for ninety days
options.B: the accused has furnished a surety and a bond
options.C: there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence on bail
options.D: the Enforcement Directorate has consented

questions.explanation: This is the text of the twin conditions as given in the passage.

questions.question: What is the effect of Najeeb and Sisodia on the stringent bail provisions of special statutes?

options.A: Only the High Court can grant bail under special statutes
options.B: The bail conditions in special statutes are struck down
options.C: Special statutes override Article 21
options.D: Prolonged incarceration without trial may justify bail despite statutory restrictions, as Article 21 prevails

questions.explanation: The passage states that constitutional courts may grant bail despite restrictions where the trial is delayed.

questions.question: Which of the following inferences is most strongly supported by the passage?

options.A: Statutory restrictions on bail operate in isolation from constitutional guarantees
options.B: Article 22(1) and Article 21 give the courts a basis to scrutinise both the manner of arrest and the length of incarceration under stringent statutes
options.C: The PMLA is unconstitutional
options.D: Bail can never be granted in special statutes

questions.explanation: The decisions rely on Articles 22(1) and 21 to control arrest procedure and prolonged detention.

passages.title: Climate Change: From the Great Indian Bustard to The Hague
passages.passage: In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court, while considering the protection of the Great Indian Bustard from overhead power lines, held that the right to life under Article 21 and the right to equality under Article 14 include a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change. The Court reasoned that without a clean environment stable in climate, the right to health and life cannot be fully realised, and that the State must balance the transition to renewable energy with the protection of endangered species. On 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice delivered a unanimous advisory opinion on the Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, in response to a request by the General Assembly prompted by Vanuatu and other small island States. The Court held that States are bound by the climate treaties, including the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, as well as by customary international law, which includes the duty to prevent significant harm to the environment and to cooperate. It held that the standard of due diligence is stringent, in view of the grave risk, and that the 1.5 degree Celsius temperature goal is the primary target under the Paris Agreement. National determined contributions must, collectively and individually, reflect the highest possible ambition. The Court added that the production and consumption of fossil fuels, the grant of exploration licences and fossil fuel subsidies may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to the State, and that such a breach entails legal consequences, including cessation, guarantees of non-repetition and full reparation, in the form of restitution, compensation or satisfaction. Although advisory opinions are not binding, they carry legal authority and are likely to be cited before national courts and in contentious proceedings.

questions.question: The Supreme Court in M.K. Ranjitsinh recognised the right against adverse effects of climate change as part of

options.A: Article 19(1)(g) only
options.B: Articles 14 and 21
options.C: Article 32 only
options.D: the Directive Principles alone

questions.explanation: The passage states that Articles 14 and 21 include this right.

questions.question: According to the ICJ opinion described, the standard of due diligence applicable to States is

options.A: applicable only to developed States
options.B: stringent, in view of the grave risk to the climate system
options.C: dependent only on the State's wishes
options.D: minimal, as climate is a global matter

questions.explanation: The passage states that the due diligence standard is stringent.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated as a possible legal consequence of an internationally wrongful act in the passage?

options.A: Guarantees of non-repetition
options.B: Full reparation
options.C: Automatic expulsion from the United Nations
options.D: Cessation

questions.explanation: Cessation, non-repetition and reparation are listed; expulsion from the UN is not.

questions.question: The legal status of the ICJ's advisory opinion is best described as

options.A: not binding in itself, but carrying legal authority and likely to be cited
options.B: of no value
options.C: binding only on Vanuatu
options.D: binding on all States as a judgment

questions.explanation: The passage states advisory opinions are not binding but carry authority.

questions.question: A State grants fresh licences for coal exploration, despite its commitments under the Paris Agreement. On the passage, the ICJ's reasoning suggests that this

options.A: may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to the State
options.B: is a purely domestic matter
options.C: is permitted as long as the State submits its NDC
options.D: is relevant only for contentious cases between neighbours

questions.explanation: The Court held that the grant of exploration licences may constitute an internationally wrongful act.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best inference connecting the two decisions?

options.A: Both treat climate protection as a matter of moral exhortation, without legal content
options.B: Both treat climate protection as carrying binding legal obligations, one grounded in fundamental rights at the national level and the other in treaty and customary duties at the international level
options.C: Both hold that renewable energy has priority over all other interests
options.D: Both are advisory opinions

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court tied it to Articles 14 and 21; the ICJ tied it to treaty and customary law.

passages.title: Arbitration: Non-signatories, Stamping and Limits of Court Intervention
passages.passage: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as amended in 2015 and 2019, seeks to limit judicial intervention in arbitral proceedings. Section 34 allows a party to apply to set aside an award on narrow grounds, including incapacity, invalid agreement, want of notice, an award beyond the scope of the submission, and conflict with the public policy of India, which now includes fraud, corruption, violation of fundamental policy of Indian law and conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice. An award in a domestic arbitration may also be set aside for 'patent illegality appearing on the face of the award', though not by mere erroneous application of law or re-appreciation of evidence. In Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft Technologies (2025), a Constitution Bench held by a majority of four to one that although Section 34 confers on courts the power to set aside, and not to modify, an award, a limited power of modification exists: courts may correct clerical, computational or typographical errors, sever the invalid portion from the valid portion of an award and modify post-award interest; the Supreme Court may, in rare cases, use Article 142 but only with great caution. In Cox and Kings Ltd v. SAP India Pvt Ltd (2023), a Constitution Bench held that the 'group of companies' doctrine can be applied to bind non-signatory affiliates to an arbitration agreement, where there is a mutual intention of the parties to do so, to be gathered from factors such as the conduct of the parties and the commonality of the subject matter. In In Re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration Act and the Stamp Act (2023), a seven-judge Bench held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void or void ab initio, but inadmissible in evidence, a defect curable by payment of stamp duty. Courts at the referral stage under Section 11 should confine themselves to examining the existence of an arbitration agreement on a prima facie basis, leaving other questions to the tribunal under the principle of competence-competence.

questions.question: Under the passage, which of the following is NOT a power of a court under Section 34, as clarified in Gayatri Balasamy?

options.A: To correct computational or typographical errors in the award
options.B: To set aside an award on the statutory grounds
options.C: To re-appreciate the evidence and substitute its own view on merits
options.D: To sever the invalid portion from the valid portion of an award

questions.explanation: The passage states that re-appreciation of evidence is not permitted; the other options are within the limited power.

questions.question: A non-signatory affiliate of a signatory company is sought to be bound to the arbitration clause. Following Cox and Kings, the decisive test is

options.A: whether the main contract has been stamped
options.B: whether the affiliate is part of the same group, irrespective of intent
options.C: whether the affiliate holds shares in the signatory
options.D: whether there was a mutual intention to bind the non-signatory, gathered from conduct and the commonality of the subject matter

questions.explanation: The doctrine applies only where mutual intention exists.

questions.question: The Seven-Judge Bench held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is

options.A: enforceable only before the High Court
options.B: valid and admissible without any duty
options.C: void ab initio
options.D: inadmissible in evidence but curable by payment of duty

questions.explanation: The passage states it is not void, but inadmissible, a curable defect.

questions.question: At the Section 11 stage, the court is expected to

options.A: decide the merits of the dispute
options.B: examine whether the claim is time-barred in all cases
options.C: examine the existence of the arbitration agreement on a prima facie basis
options.D: decide the validity of the main contract

questions.explanation: The referral court's role is limited under competence-competence.

questions.question: An award contains a clear arithmetical error in computing interest and also awards a sum in respect of a matter not submitted to arbitration, severable from the rest. Based on Gayatri Balasamy, the court may

options.A: re-write the award to the court's own assessment
options.B: correct the computational error and sever the portion beyond the submission, leaving the remainder intact
options.C: set aside the entire award in all cases
options.D: do nothing, as the court has no power to modify

questions.explanation: Correction of computational errors and severance are within the limited power recognised.

questions.question: The overall policy that emerges from the passage is best described as

options.A: preference of litigation over arbitration
options.B: minimal and carefully calibrated court intervention, respecting the tribunal's competence
options.C: maximum court supervision over arbitration
options.D: complete exclusion of court involvement

questions.explanation: All the decisions indicate limited intervention and respect for the tribunal.

passages.title: Free Consent, Restraint of Trade and Liquidated Damages
passages.passage: Under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement is a contract if made by the free consent of competent parties for a lawful consideration and object, and not expressly declared void. Under Section 14, consent is not free when caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. Where consent is caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, the contract is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Under Section 16, a contract is induced by undue influence where the relations between the parties are such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage. The courts have recognised, as in Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986), that unconscionable contracts, where bargaining power is grossly unequal, may be struck down as contrary to public policy under Section 23. Section 27 declares void every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business, with a narrow exception for the sale of the goodwill of a business. In Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. Century Spinning (1967), the Supreme Court distinguished between a covenant operative during the term of employment, which is valid, and one operative after the termination of the contract, which, if in restraint of trade, is void under Section 27. On breach, Section 73 awards compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things or that the parties knew likely to result. Section 74 provides that where a sum is named as payable upon breach, the party complaining is entitled to receive 'reasonable compensation' not exceeding the amount so named, whether or not actual damage is proved, though the Supreme Court in Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA (2015) held that the party must still show that some loss was caused, except where loss is impossible to prove.

questions.question: An agreement obtained by undue influence is, under the passage,

options.A: void ab initio
options.B: valid and binding
options.C: illegal and punishable
options.D: voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused

questions.explanation: The passage states such a contract is voidable at that party's option.

questions.question: An employee in a bank agrees, in his contract, not to work for any competitor for five years after he leaves. On the principle in Golikari, this post-termination covenant is

options.A: valid, since it is part of the contract
options.B: valid only if the employer pays compensation
options.C: void, to the extent it is in restraint of trade under Section 27
options.D: valid if the employee is highly paid

questions.explanation: Post-termination restraints are void under Section 27; only restraints during employment are valid.

questions.question: Which of the following is the exception to Section 27 mentioned in the passage?

options.A: Employment contracts
options.B: Partnership between two firms
options.C: Sale of goodwill of a business
options.D: Agency contracts

questions.explanation: The passage identifies the sale of goodwill as the narrow exception.

questions.question: A contract of loan names Rs 5 lakh as payable upon breach. The lender proves no loss at all, though loss was capable of proof. Following Kailash Nath, the lender

options.A: is entitled to nothing in any event
options.B: is entitled to Rs 5 lakh automatically
options.C: is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding Rs 5 lakh only on showing that some loss was caused
options.D: may recover double the sum

questions.explanation: Section 74 requires some loss to be shown, unless proof is impossible.

questions.question: The Brojo Nath Ganguly decision illustrates that

options.A: unconscionable contracts arising from grossly unequal bargaining power can be struck down as against public policy
options.B: only legislation can regulate contract terms
options.C: freedom of contract is absolute
options.D: courts have no power to interfere with standard-form contracts

questions.explanation: The passage states that such contracts may be struck down under Section 23.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a vitiating factor of free consent under Section 14 as set out in the passage?

options.A: Inadequacy of consideration
options.B: Mistake
options.C: Coercion
options.D: Misrepresentation

questions.explanation: Inadequacy of consideration is not a ground in Section 14.

passages.title: Strict and Absolute Liability, and Professional Negligence
passages.passage: Under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), a person who for his own purposes brings and keeps on his land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is liable, without proof of negligence, for the damage that is the natural consequence of its escape. The rule is subject to exceptions, including an act of God, the act of a stranger, the plaintiff's consent or default, and statutory authority. After the Oleum gas leak in Delhi, the Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) declined to follow the exceptions to the rule and evolved the principle of absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity: such an enterprise is absolutely liable to compensate all those affected by an accident, and none of the exceptions applies. The Court added that the quantum of compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise, so that it has a deterrent effect. The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 imposes no-fault liability for hazardous substances, and the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 empowers the Tribunal to award relief and compensation in environmental cases. In the context of negligence, the test in Donoghue v. Stevenson asks whether the defendant owed a duty of care to a neighbour, one who is closely and directly affected by his acts. In professional negligence, the Bolam test asks whether the professional acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of professionals. For criminal liability of doctors, the Supreme Court in Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) held that the negligence must be 'gross', beyond mere lack of care, and that a private complaint should not be entertained unless supported by the credible opinion of another competent doctor.

questions.question: Which of the following exceptions, available under Rylands v. Fletcher, does NOT apply to an enterprise under the rule of absolute liability?

options.A: Act of God
options.B: Default of the plaintiff
options.C: Act of a stranger
options.D: All of the above

questions.explanation: The passage states that none of the exceptions applies under absolute liability.

questions.question: The Supreme Court's reasoning on the quantum of compensation in M.C. Mehta was that it should

options.A: be nominal
options.B: be proportional to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise, with a deterrent effect
options.C: be capped at the value of the plaintiff's property
options.D: be fixed by the enterprise

questions.explanation: The Court correlated compensation with the enterprise's capacity.

questions.question: A chemical factory stores toxic gas which escapes due to sabotage by an unknown third party, injuring neighbours. Under the rule of absolute liability as described, the factory is

options.A: liable, since no exception applies to a hazardous enterprise
options.B: not liable, since the act of a stranger is a defence
options.C: liable only if it was negligent
options.D: liable only to the extent of the insurance cover

questions.explanation: Under absolute liability, no exception, including that of a stranger, applies.

questions.question: The Bolam test is concerned with whether the professional

options.A: obtained the patient's written consent
options.B: charged reasonable fees
options.C: acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of professionals
options.D: took the highest possible care

questions.explanation: This is the Bolam test as set out in the passage.

questions.question: A patient files a private criminal complaint against a surgeon for negligence without any medical opinion. In line with Jacob Mathew, the complaint

options.A: should not ordinarily be entertained without the credible opinion of another competent doctor
options.B: must be entertained as of right
options.C: must be treated as a case of murder
options.D: must be transferred to a civil court

questions.explanation: Jacob Mathew requires a prima facie opinion of another competent doctor.

questions.question: Which of the following statements best states the difference between strict liability and absolute liability as derived from the passage?

options.A: There is no difference
options.B: Strict liability applies only to enterprises
options.C: Absolute liability is limited to the value of the property
options.D: Strict liability has exceptions and absolute liability has none

questions.explanation: The passage notes that the Court refused to follow the exceptions to Rylands v. Fletcher.

passages.title: Artificial Intelligence, Authorship and Patentability
passages.passage: Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957 confers copyright on original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Section 2(d)(vi) provides that, in relation to any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work which is computer-generated, the 'author' is the person who causes the work to be created. The Supreme Court in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008) rejected both the 'sweat of the brow' and the 'creativity' extremes, and adopted the 'modicum of creativity' standard, holding that a work must involve some intellectual effort and skill, more than mere labour, to qualify as original. The rise of generative artificial intelligence has presented two questions to the courts and legislators: whether output generated by an AI model is protectable, and whether the use of copyrighted material to train such models infringes the copyright. In Asian News International v. OpenAI, pending before the Delhi High Court, the news agency alleges that its articles were used without licence to train a large language model and reproduced in its outputs; the defendant claims that the training involves non-expressive processing and is not infringement, and questions arise on the application of the closed list of exceptions in Section 52, which includes fair dealing for private use, research, criticism, review and reporting of current events. Separately, Section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes from patentability a 'computer programme per se', and mathematical or business methods. In Ferid Allani v. Union of India (2019), the Delhi High Court held that computer-related inventions which demonstrate a 'technical effect' or 'technical contribution' are not excluded merely because they involve a computer programme. Several High Courts have also granted personality-rights injunctions to well-known persons against the use of their name, image or voice in AI-generated content without consent.

questions.question: Under Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act as described, the author of a computer-generated work is

options.A: the computer
options.B: no one, as the work is not protected
options.C: the programmer of the software in all cases
options.D: the person who causes the work to be created

questions.explanation: The passage states this directly.

questions.question: The standard of originality adopted in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak is

options.A: a modicum of creativity involving intellectual effort and skill
options.B: sweat of the brow
options.C: creative genius
options.D: novelty and non-obviousness

questions.explanation: The Court adopted the modicum of creativity standard.

questions.question: Which of the following is the legal question raised in the ANI v. OpenAI litigation, as described in the passage?

options.A: Whether news can be copyrighted at all
options.B: Whether OpenAI may register a trademark
options.C: Whether the use of copyrighted works to train an AI model and the reproduction of such works in outputs infringes copyright, having regard to the closed list of exceptions in Section 52
options.D: Whether a large language model can hold a patent

questions.explanation: The passage describes the allegations and the issue of the Section 52 exceptions.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about patentability of computer-related inventions?

options.A: A computer programme per se is excluded, but one showing a technical effect or contribution may be patentable
options.B: Software is always patentable
options.C: All inventions involving software are excluded by Section 3(k)
options.D: Business methods are always patentable

questions.explanation: Ferid Allani held that technical effect inventions are not excluded merely because they involve a programme.

questions.question: The list of exceptions in Section 52 is described in the passage as 'closed'. The consequence is that

options.A: all uses of copyrighted works are exempt
options.B: there are no exceptions in Indian law
options.C: a use not falling within the listed exceptions cannot claim exemption under Section 52, though a court may construe the listed heads
options.D: courts may add new exceptions freely, such as AI training

questions.explanation: A closed list restricts exemptions to those enumerated, leaving interpretation of the listed heads to courts.

questions.question: A person's voice is cloned by an AI tool and used in a commercial advertisement without his consent. The most suitable legal route indicated in the passage is

options.A: no remedy is available
options.B: a personality-rights action for an injunction
options.C: a challenge to the Copyright Act
options.D: a patent infringement action

questions.explanation: The passage notes that High Courts have granted personality-rights injunctions in such cases.

passages.title: Divorce, Maintenance and the Move Towards Uniformity
passages.passage: Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows divorce by mutual consent on a joint petition after the parties have lived separately for a year, with a further period of six months between the first motion and the second motion. In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017), the Supreme Court held that the six-month period is directory and may be waived by the court in appropriate cases. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023), a Constitution Bench held that the Court may, in exercise of its power under Article 142, dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown, even though this is not a ground for divorce under the Act, where the marriage is wholly unworkable, emotionally dead and beyond salvage, but that the power should be exercised with care and not as a matter of right; the Bench also laid down factors such as the duration of the marriage, the nature of allegations and the attempts at settlement. In Rajnesh v. Neha (2020), the Court issued guidelines on maintenance, including the filing of an affidavit of disclosure of assets by both parties, and held that maintenance should be awarded from the date of the application. In Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana (2024), the Court held that a divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 144 of the BNSS), irrespective of her personal law, and that the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 does not displace that remedy. The State of Uttarakhand enacted the Uniform Civil Code, 2024, which came into force in January 2025, requiring the registration of marriages and live-in relationships; critics argue that the State lacks exclusive competence, since personal law falls in Entry 5 of the Concurrent List, while supporters rely on Article 44 of the Constitution.

questions.question: The effect of Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur on the six-month period under Section 13B is that it is

options.A: directory, and may be waived in appropriate cases
options.B: mandatory and cannot be waived
options.C: abolished altogether
options.D: applicable only to Muslims

questions.explanation: The passage states the period is directory and waivable.

questions.question: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage, in the passage, is

options.A: a ground only before family courts
options.B: a statutory ground for divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act
options.C: not a statutory ground, but the Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on this basis under Article 142, with care
options.D: a ground available to every spouse as of right

questions.explanation: Shilpa Sailesh permits the use of Article 142 and cautions against treating it as a right.

questions.question: According to Rajnesh v. Neha, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Maintenance is never payable before the final order
options.B: Both parties must file an affidavit of disclosure of assets, and maintenance is awarded from the date of the application
options.C: Only the husband files the affidavit
options.D: Maintenance is capped by statute

questions.explanation: The passage records both directions.

questions.question: A divorced Muslim woman applies for maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. On the basis of Samad, her claim is

options.A: maintainable only under the 1986 Act
options.B: barred by personal law
options.C: maintainable irrespective of her personal law
options.D: maintainable only if she has no children

questions.explanation: The Court held that Section 125 is available irrespective of personal law.

questions.question: The principal ground of criticism of the Uttarakhand UCC in the passage is that

options.A: it violates Article 44
