options.B: it applies to all of India
options.C: the State lacks exclusive competence as personal law is on the Concurrent List
options.D: it does not provide for any registration

questions.explanation: The passage records this as the critics' argument.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best summary of the trend in the passage?

options.A: Courts have used flexible interpretive and constitutional tools to prevent hardship in matrimonial disputes, while legislatures consider uniformity
options.B: Courts have prohibited maintenance
options.C: Courts have rigidly applied statutory waiting periods
options.D: Parliament has abolished divorce

questions.explanation: The passage shows judicial flexibility and legislative debate on uniformity.

passages.title: Remission, Life Imprisonment and the Appropriate Government
passages.passage: Articles 72 and 161 of the Constitution empower the President and the Governor to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions, and to suspend, remit or commute sentences. Statutory remission is regulated by Section 432 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 473 of the BNSS), under which the 'appropriate Government' may remit the sentence, subject to Section 433A, which requires a person sentenced to life for an offence punishable with death to serve at least fourteen years. In Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2016), a Constitution Bench held that life imprisonment means imprisonment for the remainder of the convict's natural life, subject to remission, and that the Supreme Court and High Courts may impose a fixed term of more than fourteen years, or a term without remission, as a substitute for the death penalty. In the Bilkis Bano case (Bilkis Yakub Rasool v. Union of India, January 2024), the Supreme Court quashed the orders of the Gujarat Government remitting the sentences of eleven convicts who had been sentenced to life for gang rape and murder during the 2002 riots. It held that the 'appropriate Government' for the purpose of remission is the State within whose territory the convict was sentenced, not the State where the offence occurred, and that, since the trial had been transferred to Maharashtra by the Supreme Court, the State of Maharashtra alone could have considered remission. The Court also held that an earlier order in the case directing Gujarat to consider remission had been obtained by suppression of material facts and was a fraud on the Court, and that the discretion to grant remission is subject to judicial review and must be exercised on relevant considerations and in a non-arbitrary manner. In Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014), the Court held that an unexplained and inordinate delay in the disposal of a mercy petition is a ground for commutation of the death sentence.

questions.question: According to V. Sriharan, life imprisonment means

options.A: twenty years' imprisonment
options.B: imprisonment for the remainder of the natural life of the convict, subject to remission
options.C: imprisonment which is automatically commuted after fourteen years
options.D: fourteen years' imprisonment

questions.explanation: The passage states this principle.

questions.question: In Bilkis Bano, the Court held that the appropriate Government for remission is

options.A: the State within whose territory the convict was sentenced
options.B: the State of the victim's residence
options.C: the State in which the offence occurred
options.D: the Union Government

questions.explanation: The Court held that it is the State where the trial took place and sentence was passed; here, Maharashtra.

questions.question: The reason the Court gave for quashing the earlier order directing Gujarat to consider remission was that it

options.A: was passed by the wrong Bench
options.B: was contrary to Article 161
options.C: was obtained by suppression of material facts and amounted to a fraud on the Court
options.D: was passed after fourteen years

questions.explanation: The passage records the finding of suppression and fraud.

questions.question: Which of the following is a ground for commutation of a death sentence as described in the passage?

options.A: The conviction by a High Court
options.B: The age of the victim
options.C: Unexplained and inordinate delay in the disposal of a mercy petition
options.D: The offender's good behaviour in the prison

questions.explanation: Shatrughan Chauhan treats such delay as a ground for commutation.

questions.question: A court wishes to substitute the death penalty with a sentence of thirty years without remission. According to the passage,

options.A: it lacks power to do so
options.B: only the legislature may do so
options.C: only the President may do so
options.D: the Supreme Court and High Courts may impose a fixed term exceeding fourteen years or without remission as an alternative to death

questions.explanation: Sriharan permits constitutional courts to impose such sentences.

questions.question: Which proposition best reflects the effect of the Bilkis Bano decision on remission powers?

options.A: Remission is a discretion subject to judicial review and must be exercised by the competent Government on relevant considerations
options.B: Remission is an unreviewable executive favour
options.C: Remission can be granted only by the President
options.D: Remission cannot be granted in cases of rape

questions.explanation: The Court held remission to be reviewable and tied to the appropriate Government.

passages.title: The Four Labour Codes
passages.passage: On 21 November 2025, the Union Government brought into force the four Labour Codes, namely the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, consolidating twenty-nine central labour laws. The Code on Wages provides for a statutory floor wage, universalises the entitlement to minimum wages and timely payment, and defines 'wages' so that, in general, remuneration components other than specified exclusions must not exceed fifty per cent of the total remuneration, which expands the wage base for calculation of benefits. The Industrial Relations Code raises the threshold for prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure from one hundred to three hundred workers, requires a notice of fourteen days for a strike in all establishments, and recognises 'fixed-term employment' on terms equal to permanent workers, with eligibility for gratuity after one year of service rather than five. The Code on Social Security for the first time defines 'gig worker' and 'platform worker' and requires aggregators to contribute a percentage of annual turnover, subject to a ceiling on the payments made to such workers, to a social security fund. The Occupational Safety Code permits women to work night shifts with their consent and with safety measures, and requires employers to offer free annual health check-ups to workers above a specified age. Trade unions have criticised the Codes for easing retrenchment and restricting strikes, while the Government states that they would formalise employment, simplify compliance and extend social security.

questions.question: The threshold for prior government permission for retrenchment under the Industrial Relations Code is

options.A: one hundred workers
options.B: two hundred workers
options.C: five hundred workers
options.D: three hundred workers

questions.explanation: The passage states that it is raised from 100 to 300.

questions.question: A fixed-term employee completes one year of service. Under the Codes, as described, he is eligible for

options.A: gratuity
options.B: only wages
options.C: no benefit until five years
options.D: pension

questions.explanation: Fixed-term employees are eligible for gratuity after one year.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly reflects the rule regarding 'wages' in the Code on Wages?

options.A: Wages exclude all allowances
options.B: Excluded components generally must not exceed fifty per cent of the total remuneration, thereby widening the wage base
options.C: Basic pay must be at least ninety per cent of remuneration
options.D: Allowances may form any proportion of total remuneration

questions.explanation: The passage states the fifty per cent rule.

questions.question: The Code on Social Security, in relation to gig and platform workers, provides that

options.A: only the Government contributes
options.B: workers contribute the whole amount
options.C: aggregators contribute a percentage of annual turnover, subject to a cap linked to payments to such workers, to a fund
options.D: they are excluded from all benefits

questions.explanation: The passage describes the aggregator contribution subject to a ceiling.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated as a feature of the Codes in the passage?

options.A: Free annual health check-up above a specified age
options.B: Night shifts for women with consent
options.C: Abolition of trade unions
options.D: Fourteen days' notice for strike in all establishments

questions.explanation: Abolition of unions is not mentioned; criticism is that strikes are restricted.

questions.question: The main criticism of trade unions about the Codes, as per the passage, is that they

options.A: increase minimum wages excessively
options.B: apply only to government employees
options.C: ease retrenchment and restrict strikes
options.D: abolish gratuity

questions.explanation: The passage records this criticism.

passages.title: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: Creditors, Clean Slate and Commercial Wisdom
passages.passage: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) provides for a time-bound resolution of the insolvency of corporate debtors. A financial creditor may initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) under Section 7, an operational creditor under Section 9, and the corporate debtor itself under Section 10. On admission, a moratorium under Section 14 prohibits the institution or continuation of suits and the enforcement of security against the debtor. An interim resolution professional takes control, and a committee of creditors (CoC), comprising financial creditors, is constituted. Section 29A bars certain persons, including wilful defaulters and persons whose accounts have been classified as non-performing assets for a specified period, from submitting a resolution plan; the Supreme Court in Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India (2019) upheld the constitutional validity of the Code, and in ArcelorMittal India v. Satish Kumar Gupta (2019) held that Section 29A applies to the resolution applicant and persons connected with him. In K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank (2019), the Court held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable and that the adjudicating authority cannot interfere with the merits of the decision to approve a resolution plan, though it may examine whether the plan complies with the statutory requirements. In Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta (2019), the Court held that the CoC may differentiate between classes of creditors, but that the equitable treatment of similarly situated creditors is to be observed. In Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction (2021), the Court held that once a resolution plan is approved by the adjudicating authority, all claims not part of the plan stand extinguished, giving the successful applicant a 'clean slate', so that it can start without undecided claims. Where no plan is approved, the corporate debtor goes into liquidation, in which the proceeds are distributed under the waterfall in Section 53.

questions.question: Which of the following may initiate CIRP under Section 9 of the Code?

options.A: A shareholder
options.B: An operational creditor
options.C: The corporate debtor
options.D: A financial creditor

questions.explanation: The passage states that an operational creditor initiates under Section 9.

questions.question: The principal effect of the moratorium under Section 14 is that

options.A: the debtor's assets vest in the Government
options.B: the debtor must pay all debts at once
options.C: the CoC is dissolved
options.D: suits and enforcement of security against the debtor are barred during CIRP

questions.explanation: The passage states this effect.

questions.question: According to K. Sashidhar, the adjudicating authority

options.A: cannot interfere with the commercial wisdom of the CoC, though it may check statutory compliance
options.B: has no role in approving a resolution plan
options.C: must approve every plan
options.D: may substitute its own view for the commercial wisdom of the CoC

questions.explanation: The Court held commercial wisdom to be non-justiciable subject to statutory compliance review.

questions.question: The 'clean slate' principle in Ghanashyam Mishra means that

options.A: claims not part of the approved plan stand extinguished
options.B: the creditors may file fresh claims at any time
options.C: the plan is subject to renewal each year
options.D: the resolution applicant is liable for all past debts

questions.explanation: This is the principle as described in the passage.

questions.question: A company's promoter, a wilful defaulter, proposes a resolution plan through a related entity. Under the passage, the plan is

options.A: permissible, since he is not the applicant
options.B: barred, as Section 29A applies to the applicant and persons connected with him
options.C: permissible if the plan pays all creditors in full
options.D: permissible only with the approval of the CoC

questions.explanation: ArcelorMittal held that Section 29A extends to connected persons.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct inference about the CoC's power to differentiate between creditors, from Essar Steel?

options.A: The CoC must treat all creditors identically
options.B: The CoC has no power over distribution
options.C: The CoC may differentiate between classes of creditors, but must ensure the equitable treatment of similarly situated creditors
options.D: The CoC has unrestricted power to discriminate

questions.explanation: The passage states the qualified power.

passages.title: Confessions, Discovery, Dying Declarations and Circumstantial Evidence
passages.passage: A confession made to a police officer is inadmissible against the accused under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (and the corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023), and a confession made while in police custody is inadmissible unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. This protection arises from the fear that confessions to the police may be extracted by coercion. The proviso, Section 27, provides that so much of the information received from the accused in custody, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered, may be proved. In Pulukuri Kottaya v. King Emperor (1947), the Privy Council explained that the 'fact discovered' embraces the place from which the object is produced and the knowledge of the accused as to this, and that only the information distinctly connected with the discovery is admissible, not the whole statement. A dying declaration is admissible under Section 32(1) as a statement made by a person as to the cause of his death or the circumstances of the transaction resulting in his death, and in Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002), a Constitution Bench held that a dying declaration is not invalid merely because it was not recorded by a Magistrate or lacks a certificate of the doctor as to fitness of mind, though the court must be satisfied that it is voluntary and truthful. Under Section 101, the burden of proving a fact lies on the person who asserts it, but Section 106 provides that where a fact is especially within the knowledge of a person, the burden of proving it lies on him; this does not relieve the prosecution of its primary burden, as the Supreme Court has stressed. In Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984), the Court laid down that in a case of circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully established, be consistent only with the guilt of the accused and form a chain so complete that no reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with his innocence remains.

questions.question: An accused in police custody tells the Investigating Officer, 'I killed him and hid the knife under the bridge'. The knife is recovered from under the bridge. Which part is admissible under Section 27?

options.A: The entire statement
options.B: Only the part that he killed the deceased
options.C: Only the part that relates distinctly to the discovery, i.e. the place of concealment of the knife
options.D: None of it

questions.explanation: Only the portion distinctly relating to the fact discovered is admissible; the confession of the killing is inadmissible.

questions.question: According to Laxman v. State of Maharashtra, a dying declaration

options.A: is invalid if the declarant survives
options.B: is not invalid merely because it was not recorded by a Magistrate or lacks a medical certificate, if the court is satisfied that it is voluntary and truthful
options.C: is invalid unless recorded by a Magistrate
options.D: requires corroboration in every case

questions.explanation: This is the holding stated in the passage.

questions.question: Section 106 of the Evidence Act, as described, means that

options.A: the court must presume guilt
options.B: the prosecution is relieved of proof in all cases
options.C: the accused must prove his innocence
options.D: the burden of proving a fact especially within his knowledge lies on the person, but the prosecution's primary burden remains

questions.explanation: The passage states that Section 106 does not relieve the prosecution of the primary burden.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of the chain of circumstances in Sharad Sarda?

options.A: There must be an eye-witness to the crime
options.B: They must be consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt
options.C: They must form a chain so complete that no reasonable ground for innocence remains
options.D: The circumstances must be fully established

questions.explanation: Circumstantial evidence applies where there is no eye-witness; the rest are requirements.

questions.question: A confession made by an accused in police custody before a police constable, and not in the presence of a Magistrate, is

options.A: inadmissible against the accused
options.B: admissible if recorded on video
options.C: admissible if voluntary
options.D: admissible if corroborated

questions.explanation: Under the passage, such confession is inadmissible unless made in the presence of a Magistrate.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the rationale for the exclusion of confessions to the police?

options.A: Confessions are never relevant
options.B: The fear that confessions may be extracted by coercion
options.C: The accused has no right to speak
options.D: Police officers are unreliable witnesses in all cases

questions.explanation: The passage identifies the fear of coercion as the rationale.

passages.title: Freedom of Speech: Restrictions, Incitement and Courage of Courts
passages.passage: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees to all citizens the freedom of speech and expression, and Article 19(2) permits the State to impose by law only reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act as vague and overbroad, drawing the distinction between mere discussion or advocacy, which is protected however unpopular, and incitement, which can be restricted; the Court upheld Section 69A, which allows blocking of online content, because it was accompanied by procedural safeguards, including reasons recorded in writing and a review mechanism. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), the Court held that freedom of speech on the internet and the right to carry on trade through the internet enjoy constitutional protection, that an order suspending internet services must be published and is subject to judicial review on the proportionality test, and that indefinite shutdowns are impermissible. In Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023), a Constitution Bench held that no restrictions beyond those enumerated in Article 19(2) can be imposed on the freedom of speech, and that fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 21 can, in certain circumstances, be enforced even against private persons. In Imran Pratapgarhi v. State of Gujarat (2025), the Court quashed an FIR registered over a poem posted on social media, observing that even if a large number of persons dislike the views expressed, the right of the speaker must be respected, that the effect of words must be judged by the standards of reasonable, strong-minded and courageous persons, not those of the weak and vacillating, and that the courts are duty bound to uphold the right.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a ground of restriction enumerated in Article 19(2) as set out in the passage?

options.A: Public order
options.B: Public interest in general
options.C: Decency or morality
options.D: Incitement to an offence

questions.explanation: 'Public interest' at large is not a listed ground; Kaushal Kishor confirms that no additional restrictions are permitted.

questions.question: Why was Section 66A struck down in Shreya Singhal?

options.A: Because it was vague and overbroad and impermissibly restricted discussion and advocacy
options.B: Because it applied only to journalists
options.C: Because it was passed by the wrong House
options.D: Because it lacked a review mechanism

questions.explanation: The passage states the vagueness and overbreadth ground and the distinction between advocacy and incitement.

questions.question: Section 69A was upheld in Shreya Singhal because

options.A: it had no relation to Article 19
options.B: it permitted unlimited blocking
options.C: it applied only to Government websites
options.D: it had procedural safeguards such as written reasons and review

questions.explanation: The safeguards saved the provision.

questions.question: A district magistrate suspends internet services indefinitely and does not publish the order. On the basis of Anuradha Bhasin, the order is

options.A: valid, as internet access is not a right
options.B: valid for up to one year
options.C: open to challenge, as indefinite shutdowns are impermissible and orders must be published and tested on proportionality
options.D: valid if the magistrate is satisfied

questions.explanation: The passage states the three requirements: publication, proportionality review and no indefinite suspension.

questions.question: The significance of Kaushal Kishor, as presented in the passage, is that it

options.A: holds that restrictions on speech are limited to those in Article 19(2) and that certain fundamental rights can be enforced against private persons
options.B: overrules Shreya Singhal
options.C: abolishes the right to speech against private persons
options.D: permits the State to add new grounds of restriction under Article 21

questions.explanation: This captures both limbs of the holding in the passage.

questions.question: The Court in Imran Pratapgarhi suggests that the effect of speech is to be judged by the standard of

options.A: the police officer registering the case
options.B: the most sensitive member of the audience
options.C: the majority of the public
options.D: reasonable, strong-minded and courageous persons

questions.explanation: The passage states the standard.

passages.title: Transfer of Immovable Property: Form, Possession and Notice
passages.passage: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a sale of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards can be made only by a registered instrument; the mere delivery of possession or the payment of the price does not transfer ownership, and a contract for sale does not itself create any interest in or charge on the property. Section 53A, however, protects a transferee who has taken possession in part performance of a written contract signed by the transferor, where the transferee has done some act in furtherance of the contract and is willing to perform his part; the transferor is then debarred from enforcing against him any right in respect of the property other than those expressly provided in the contract. The protection is, however, available only as a shield by way of defence, and not as a sword to claim title. In Suraj Lamp and Industries v. State of Haryana (2011), the Supreme Court held that transactions styled as sale by a General Power of Attorney, agreement to sell and will do not convey title, and cannot be recognised as completed transfers, since a sale must be by a registered deed of conveyance, although the Court clarified that its decision would not affect genuine agency arrangements and earlier transactions already acted upon. Section 52 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens: during the pendency of a suit in which the right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred so as to affect the rights of any other party, so that a transferee pendente lite is bound by the result of the suit even without notice. Section 41 protects a transferee from an ostensible owner who has acted with the consent of the real owner, where the transferee has taken reasonable care and acted in good faith.

questions.question: A buys a house from B for Rs 50 lakh, pays the entire price and takes possession, but no deed is registered. Under the passage, ownership

options.A: passed on the date of the agreement
options.B: has passed to A by delivery of possession
options.C: passed upon payment of the price
options.D: has not passed, since a sale of such property requires a registered instrument

questions.explanation: Section 54 requires a registered instrument; possession and payment alone do not pass title.

questions.question: Section 53A can be invoked by

options.A: a transferee in possession under a written contract, as a defence against the transferor
options.B: a transferee, as a ground to claim title in a suit
options.C: a transferor against a third person
options.D: any person in possession of the property

questions.explanation: The doctrine operates as a shield and not as a sword.

questions.question: The holding in Suraj Lamp is that

options.A: a GPA sale conveys good title
options.B: sales need not be registered
options.C: all GPAs are void
options.D: GPA, agreement to sell and will arrangements do not amount to a completed transfer of title

questions.explanation: The Court held that such transactions do not pass title.

questions.question: During the pendency of a suit about ownership of a plot, the defendant sells the plot to C, who has no notice of the suit. On the basis of Section 52, C

options.A: must be joined, or the suit abates
options.B: is bound by the result of the suit, even without notice
options.C: takes free of the suit
options.D: is entitled to ask for refund only

questions.explanation: The doctrine of lis pendens binds the transferee pendente lite irrespective of notice.

questions.question: Which of the following is a requirement for protection under Section 41?

options.A: The transferor must be a minor
options.B: The transfer must be gratuitous
options.C: The transferee must have taken reasonable care and acted in good faith, and the ostensible owner must have acted with the real owner's consent
options.D: The real owner must be a company

questions.explanation: The passage lists these requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is the most accurate?

options.A: Part performance gives a transferee a title as against the world
options.B: Part performance confers on the transferee a defensive right against the transferor, but title still requires a registered conveyance
options.C: Registration is optional in all sales
options.D: Lis pendens applies only if notice is served

questions.explanation: Combining Sections 54 and 53A shows that part performance is defensive and does not substitute for a registered sale deed.

passages.title: Judicial Review: Reasonableness, Proportionality, Legitimate Expectation and Tribunals
passages.passage: Judicial review of administrative action in India rests on the tests of illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. The Wednesbury test, from Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948), treats a decision as unreasonable only where it is so outrageous in its defiance of logic that no sensible person could have arrived at it. Indian courts have also developed the doctrine of proportionality, which asks whether the measure is suitable, necessary and balanced in its effect on the right affected. In Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001), the Supreme Court explained that where an administrative action affects fundamental rights, the court examines the proportionality of the action as primary reviewer, whereas in the case of other rights Wednesbury review applies, with the court confined to the decision-making process. The doctrine of legitimate expectation protects a person who has been led by a promise or a settled practice to expect a benefit; in Navjyoti Co-operative Group Housing Society v. Union of India (1992), the Court held that the expectation may be defeated only for a good public reason and after a fair hearing; it does not give a vested right. The principles of natural justice, nemo judex in causa sua and audi alteram partem, have been given an Article 14 and Article 21 basis in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), so that procedure affecting rights must be fair, just and reasonable. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that tribunals, though they can decide questions of law and fact, remain subject to the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, since judicial review is part of the basic structure. In Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2021), the Court struck down provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 prescribing a minimum age of fifty years and a four-year tenure for tribunal members, holding that they undermined judicial independence.

passages.title: Kelsen's Pure Theory, Revolutions and Legal Realism
passages.passage: Hans Kelsen's Pure Theory of Law seeks a science of law purged of political, moral and sociological elements. For Kelsen, law is a hierarchy of norms in which the validity of every norm derives from a higher norm, until the chain terminates in the Grundnorm, a hypothetical, presupposed basic norm, which is not itself posited by any authority and whose validity is assumed as a juristic hypothesis. The Grundnorm does not state what is just, but only that one ought to behave as the framers of the first constitution have ordained. A legal system must also be, by and large, efficacious, for a norm that is not effective loses its validity. Kelsen's theory was invoked in State v. Dosso (1958), where the Supreme Court of Pakistan, after a military coup, held that a successful revolution is an internationally recognised method of changing a constitution and becomes a law-creating fact; the new regime's order was thereby validated. In Asma Jilani v. Government of the Punjab (1972), the same Court rejected Dosso, holding that the Grundnorm cannot be located in an efficacious usurpation, and that Kelsen's theory had been misapplied. Legal realists, in contrast, were sceptical of rules. Oliver Wendell Holmes defined law as a prediction of what the courts will do in fact, from the viewpoint of the 'bad man' who cares only for the material consequences of his conduct. Jerome Frank, in the strand of 'fact scepticism', stressed that the uncertainty of facts found by the trial court makes the prediction of judgment unreliable, while Karl Llewellyn emphasised the 'law-in-action' over the 'law-in-books'. Hart criticised the realists for 'rule scepticism', arguing that predicting what a judge will do ignores the internal point of view from which the rule is accepted as a standard, and that the predictive account cannot explain why courts regard themselves as bound by rules.

passages.title: Treaties, Suspension and the Indus Waters Treaty
passages.passage: The law of treaties is codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 (VCLT), many of whose rules are regarded as reflecting customary international law. Article 26 embodies the principle of pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force is binding on the parties and must be performed in good faith. A party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform (Article 27). Article 56 provides that a treaty which contains no provision regarding termination or denunciation is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal, unless it is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation, or such a right is implied by the nature of the treaty. Article 60 allows a party specially affected by a material breach by another party to invoke the breach as a ground for terminating or suspending the treaty, and Article 62 permits termination only for a fundamental change of circumstances that was not foreseen and which radically transforms the obligations still to be performed; the ICJ in Gabcikovo-Nagymaros Project (Hungary/Slovakia) (1997) stressed that these grounds must be applied restrictively, in the interest of the stability of treaty relations. Article 65 prescribes a procedure of notice and, in case of objection, peaceful settlement of disputes. The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 between India and Pakistan contains no clause for unilateral termination; it provides for a Permanent Indus Commission and a graded dispute resolution mechanism comprising questions, differences and disputes, which may lead to a Neutral Expert or a Court of Arbitration. In April 2025, following a terrorist attack in Pahalgam, India announced that the treaty would be held 'in abeyance' until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures cross-border terrorism, while Pakistan described any interference with water flows as an act of war. A Court of Arbitration constituted under the treaty issued awards in 2025 asserting its competence notwithstanding the announcement, which India rejects as the proceedings in its view are illegally constituted. India is not a party to the VCLT, though it accepts many of its rules as customary.

options.A: treaties bind only upon ratification by the UN
options.B: treaties may be terminated at will
options.C: domestic law prevails over treaties
options.D: every treaty in force binds the parties and must be performed in good faith

options.C: is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal unless the parties intended such a possibility or it is implied by the nature of the treaty
options.D: terminates after fifty years

options.B: The VCLT does not apply to river treaties
options.C: Material breach and fundamental change are easily invoked

questions.question: A State claims it may suspend a treaty because of a terrorist attack attributed to the other party, without invoking Articles 60, 62 or 65 or any treaty clause. On the basis of the passage, the strongest objection is that

options.A: the State lacks sovereignty
options.B: terrorism is irrelevant in international law
options.C: the VCLT grounds are limited, require specific conditions and a procedure, and Article 27 bars reliance on internal law, so a bare unilateral 'abeyance' lacks an evident basis
options.D: the treaty must be performed only by the weaker State

questions.explanation: The VCLT confines termination or suspension to specified grounds (e.g. Articles 60 and 62), prescribes a procedure (Article 65), and Article 27 bars reliance on internal law. A bare unilateral 'abeyance' without a treaty clause or recognised ground lacks an evident legal basis. (The State may counter that the attack is a material breach, but that is an argument under Article 60, not a ground outside it.)
